site.name: Alamakee
site.componentDetail: Historic Alamakee gold mine in the Gold Hill Mining District, one of the district's early productive lodes and later part of the Gold Hill Mining Company's holdings.
overview: The Alamakee was one of the early productive lodes in the Gold Hill Mining District northwest of Boulder. It emerged during the first wave of hard-rock mining after the 1859 gold discoveries and supplied ore to early stamp-mill operations on Left Hand Creek.

The mine remained part of Gold Hill's long mining story after the easiest surface ores were exhausted. Historic records show it persisted as a recognized property through later district revivals and was still being treated as an important historic producer in the early twentieth century.

timeline.text: The Alamakee became one of the early productive lodes developed around Gold Hill during the district's first hard-rock mining boom.
Alamakee and other nearby mines supplied surface ores to stamp mills on Left Hand Creek while miners worked the district's oxidized near-surface ore.
After the first rush declined, the Alamakee remained one of the richer Gold Hill properties whose owners retained the mine while better ore-treatment technology developed.
A surviving Boulder historical photograph documents the Alamakee Mine together with the Cold Spring and Gold Ring mines in the Gold Hill area.
The Gold Hill Mining Company acquired the Alamakee along with several other formerly rich Gold Hill producers and leased some properties to small mining parties.

moreHistory: National Register documentation for the Gold Hill district identifies the Alamakee among the important historic mines retained after the easily processed free-gold ore was depleted. That history illustrates the transition from the initial rush to more technically demanding hard-rock mining.

Modern federal mining-environment documents still identify the Alamakee vein among the important mineralized structures of the Gold Hill district, showing that the property remains a recognized part of the district's geologic and mining history.

The Remnant coordinate is a historic mine-site reference for identification, not a statement that a mine opening is safe or publicly accessible. Visitors should not enter workings or cross private-property boundaries.
